title: Archaeologists Unravel an 88-Year-Old Murder Mystery - Nautilus
gist: Recounts the January 10, 1938 killing of British archaeologist James Leslie Starkey near Hebron by five armed men, and how British authorities focused on Palestinian rebel commander Issa al-Battat, later killed in a Hebron ambush; the article is truncated by a paywall before revealing archaeologists' new findings.

insights.claim: On January 10, 1938, British archaeologist James Leslie Starkey was ambushed outside Hebron by five armed men with faces covered, who released his driver and later Starkey was found dead.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Historical context on violence in Mandate Palestine during the 1930s revolt period.
insights.quote: Starkey’s driver spotted five armed men with white headscarves covering their faces

insights.claim: Starkey had been studying an ancient Canaanite and Israelite settlement (rendered in the text as Lasich) and was traveling to Jerusalem when attacked.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows how archaeological work was entangled with regional political conflict.

insights.claim: British authorities investigating the murder focused on Issa al-Battat, a Palestinian rebel commander who commanded dozens of fighters, collected protection money from villages, and had attacked a British police commander a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates insurgent financing via protection money and colonial counterinsurgency patterns.
insights.quote: collected protection money from local villages

insights.claim: Acting on a tip, British forces ambushed and killed al-Battat in Hebron after a prolonged firefight, a resolution the article's framing implies may now be questioned by archaeologists.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Revisionist historical findings can reshape narratives in contested regions.
